title: Convergence and acceleration of a nonlinear fixed-point iteration for computing the Fitness Centrality of general graphs
summary: We establish the global convergence of the (non-homogeneous) Fitness Centrality algorithm for general graphs, deriving an explicit convergence bound for the corresponding fixed-point iteration. Furthermore, we show how the convergence can be dramatically improved by Anderson acceleration and by switching to Newton's method once a sufficiently good approximation to the fixed point has been found. The efficacy of this strategy is illustrated by numerical experiments on different types of graphs.

AI.tldr: This paper proves global convergence of the Fitness Centrality algorithm for general graphs, provides an explicit convergence bound for the fixed-point iteration, and demonstrates that convergence can be dramatically accelerated using Anderson acceleration followed by Newton's method once near a fixed point, validated via numerical experiments on various graph types.
AI.motivation: The Fitness Centrality algorithm lacked rigorous convergence guarantees for general graphs, and its fixed-point iteration could be slow. The authors aim to establish theoretical convergence bounds and practical acceleration strategies.
AI.method: The authors derive an explicit convergence bound for the Fitness Centrality fixed-point iteration. They employ Anderson acceleration to speed up convergence and propose a strategy of switching to Newton's method once a sufficiently good approximation to the fixed point is available.
AI.result: Global convergence is established with explicit bounds for general graphs. The combination of Anderson acceleration and a Newton's method switch dramatically improves convergence speed, as confirmed by numerical experiments on different graph types.
AI.conclusion: The Fitness Centrality algorithm is provably globally convergent on general graphs, and its practical efficiency can be significantly enhanced through hybrid acceleration techniques.

title: A Framework Integrating the Dynamic Stiffness Matrix with Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Solving Eigenvalue Problems and Analysing Dynamic Response
summary: This paper introduces a framework that integrates the dynamic stiffness matrix (DSM) with physics-informed neural networks (PINN). The DSM-PINN embeds physical constraints within the model and demonstrates robustness, particularly when addressing limited datasets across diverse investigations. In this approach, deep neural network outputs approximate the displacement fields of element nodes. Unlike the finite element method (FEM), the element shape functions are homogeneous solutions to the governing partial differential equation, forming the basis of the exact dynamic stiffness matrix, thereby avoiding high-order derivative terms. This matrix also serves as a frequency-domain spectral element, resulting in a strong-form PINN. The loss function is produced by connecting neural networks with dynamic stiffness matrices. We focus on utilising PINNs to resolve eigenvalue problems by employing the Wittrick-Williams algorithm, which overcomes the challenge of neural networks failing to converge to higher-order eigenvalues. Additionally, the frequency domain-PINN method is used to analyse structural dynamic responses under moving and impulsive loads, addressing the limitation of neural networks in handling complex numbers. Theoretical convergence stability of the suggested approach is also analysed even DSM is an indefinite matrix after implementing the boundary condition. The numerical results validate the practicality and efficacy of the recommended approach.

AI.tldr: Proposes DSM-PINN, a framework combining dynamic stiffness matrices with physics-informed neural networks for structural analysis, embedding physical constraints to handle limited data, resolving eigenvalue problems via the Wittrick-Williams algorithm, and addressing complex-number and high-order eigenvalue convergence challenges.
AI.motivation: PINNs face challenges with higher-order eigenvalue convergence and complex numbers in structural dynamics; the authors integrate exact dynamic stiffness matrices to embed physical constraints and overcome these limitations, particularly with limited datasets.
AI.method: Neural network outputs approximate element-node displacement fields; element shape functions are homogeneous solutions to the governing PDE forming the exact dynamic stiffness matrix (avoiding high-order derivatives). The loss function connects networks with DSM matrices, creating a strong-form PINN. The Wittrick-Williams algorithm handles eigenvalue problems, and a frequency-domain approach addresses structural responses under moving/impulsive loads.
AI.result: Numerical results validate practicality and efficacy; theoretical convergence stability is established even though the DSM is an indefinite matrix after boundary conditions are applied.
AI.conclusion: The DSM-PINN framework successfully integrates spectral-element-based physical constraints into PINNs, providing robust performance with limited data and overcoming key neural network limitations in eigenvalue and complex-number structural dynamic problems.

title: Overcoming the spatial order barrier for nonlinear SPDEs with additive space-time white noise
summary: We introduce a fully discrete numerical scheme for semilinear SPDEs with additive space-time white noise that overcomes the previous order barrier for the spatial convergence rate. The scheme achieves a strong convergence rate of $M^{-1+ε}$ in time and $N^{-3/2+ε}$ in space for any $ε>0$, where $M^{-1}$ and $N^{-1}$ are the temporal, respectively the spatial, meshsizes. This substantially improves the standard spatial error bounds of order $N^{-1/2}$ in the literature.

AI.tldr: A novel fully discrete numerical scheme for semilinear SPDEs with additive space-time white noise achieves strong convergence rates of M^{-1+ε} in time and N^{-3/2+ε} in space, dramatically improving the previous best spatial rate of N^{-1/2}.
AI.motivation: Existing numerical schemes for semilinear SPDEs with additive space-time white noise are limited by a spatial convergence rate barrier of order N^{-1/2}, which is suboptimal and restricts the practical accuracy of simulations.
AI.method: The paper introduces a fully discrete numerical scheme designed to break the previous spatial convergence order barrier, achieving improved rates in both temporal and spatial discretization.
AI.result: The scheme achieves strong convergence rates of M^{-1+ε} in time and N^{-3/2+ε} in space for any ε>0, significantly improving upon the standard spatial error bound of N^{-1/2} found in existing literature.
AI.conclusion: The proposed scheme overcomes the long-standing spatial convergence barrier for semilinear SPDEs with additive space-time white noise, providing substantially better error bounds than previously available methods.

title: Separable Nonnegative Matrix Factorization Using Powered Ratio-of-Norms Regularization
summary: Separable nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF) has been widely used for low-rank representation and clustering of nonnegative data, owing to its ability to produce part-based and interpretable decompositions. In particular, SNMF is closely related to graph clustering and community detection. To enhance sparsity and identifiability of the learned factors, we propose an $\ell_1^p/\ell_2$-regularized SNMF model based on a powered ratio-of-norms regularizer. The resulting formulation is nonconvex and nonsmooth, which poses significant challenges for optimization. To address this, we develop efficient algorithms based on the difference-of-convex function algorithm (DCA) and the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM). The proposed methods decompose the original problem into tractable subproblems, leveraging closed-form proximal operators associated with the powered norm terms. We establish descent and limiting criticality properties for the DCA scheme and convergence under standard assumptions for the ADMM scheme. Extensive numerical experiments on synthetic datasets and hand gesture classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves competitive or improved performance in anchor identification and classification accuracy compared with existing SNMF methods, while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes an ℓ₁ᵖ/ℓ₂-regularized separable nonnegative matrix factorization (SNMF) model using a powered ratio-of-norms regularizer to enhance sparsity and identifiability, solved via DCA and ADMM algorithms with closed-form proximal operators, demonstrating competitive performance in anchor identification and classification.
AI.motivation: SNMF is widely used for low-rank representation and clustering of nonnegative data, but existing methods lack sufficient sparsity and identifiability guarantees in the learned factors.
AI.method: Proposes an ℓ₁ᵖ/ℓ₂-regularized SNMF model with a powered ratio-of-norms regularizer, and develops optimization algorithms based on difference-of-convex function algorithm (DCA) and alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), leveraging closed-form proximal operators for tractable subproblems.
AI.result: Extensive numerical experiments on synthetic datasets and hand gesture classification demonstrate competitive or improved performance in anchor identification and classification accuracy compared with existing SNMF methods, while maintaining competitive computational efficiency.
AI.conclusion: The proposed regularized SNMF approach with DCA/ADMM solvers achieves enhanced sparsity and identifiability, with established convergence guarantees and practical performance gains.

title: ELMO: An Uncertainty-Aware Simulation-to-Surrogate Workflow for Fast Pedestal Linear-Stability Prediction
summary:
Rapid prediction of pedestal linear stability is important for exploring tokamak operating space, uncertainty quantification, and future model-informed control, but mode-resolved magnetohydrodynamic stability calculations using BOUT++ are computationally expensive. We present a focused implementation of ELMO--the Edge Learning and Modeling Orchestrator--as an uncertainty-aware simulation-to-surrogate workflow integrating equilibrium generation, field-aligned mesh construction, large-scale BOUT++ calculations, automated campaign execution and data reduction, and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR).
  For a single DIII-D plasma shape, 3,869 of 7,992 requested configurations completed equilibrium reconstruction, mesh generation, stability calculation, and quality control. Each retained equilibrium was evaluated at sixteen toroidal mode numbers, $n=5$--80 with $Δn=5$, using ideal-MHD and ideal-plus-diamagnetic models, producing 123,808 mode-resolved calculations. Using eight pedestal features, the GPR surrogate predicts two sixteen-mode growth-rate spectra with latent posterior uncertainty estimates.
  Across five independent test realizations, the maximum-growth-rate prediction achieved $R^2=0.978\pm0.013$ for ideal MHD and $R^2=0.966\pm0.009$ for ideal-plus-diamagnetic physics. The surrogate reproduces the spectral shape and dominant unstable mode. Calibration diagnostics indicate that posterior uncertainties are useful for relative acquisition but are underdispersed and should not be interpreted as calibrated prediction intervals. Prediction of all 32 outputs requires about 20 ms on one CPU core, compared with about 21 min using 128 CPU cores for the corresponding BOUT++ scan, giving a $6.3\times10^4$-fold wall-clock speedup and an $8.1\times10^6$-fold reduction in computational cost.

AI.tldr: This paper presents ELMO, an uncertainty-aware simulation-to-surrogate workflow for rapidly predicting pedestal linear stability in tokamaks. It combines equilibrium generation, mesh construction, large-scale BOUT++ MHD stability calculations, and Gaussian Process Regression to predict growth-rate spectra across 16 toroidal mode numbers, achieving a ~6.3×10⁴-fold wall-clock speedup compared to direct BOUT++ simulations.
AI.motivation: Mode-resolved magnetohydrodynamic stability calculations using BOUT++ are computationally expensive, which limits their use in exploring tokamak operating space, uncertainty quantification, and model-informed control. A fast surrogate is needed to enable real-time or rapid prediction of pedestal stability.
AI.method: ELMO integrates equilibrium generation, field-aligned mesh construction, large-scale BOUT++ stability calculations, automated campaign execution and data reduction, and Gaussian Process Regression (GPR). For a single DIII-D plasma shape, 3,869 configurations were evaluated at 16 toroidal mode numbers (n=5-80) using ideal-MHD and ideal-plus-diamagnetic models, producing 123,808 mode-resolved calculations. A GPR surrogate was trained using eight pedestal features to predict the two sixteen-mode growth-rate spectra with latent posterior uncertainty estimates.
AI.result: The surrogate achieved R²=0.978±0.013 for ideal MHD and R²=0.966±0.009 for ideal-plus-diamagnetic physics across five independent test realizations. It reproduces spectral shape and dominant unstable mode. Posterior uncertainties are underdispersed (useful for relative acquisition but not calibrated prediction intervals). Prediction of all 32 outputs takes ~20 ms on one CPU core versus ~21 min on 128 cores for BOUT++, yielding a 6.3×10⁴-fold wall-clock speedup and 8.1×10⁶-fold computational cost reduction.
AI.conclusion: ELMO demonstrates an effective end-to-end workflow for training fast, uncertainty-aware surrogates of pedestal stability. While the surrogate is highly accurate for growth-rate prediction and offers dramatic computational savings, the uncertainty estimates require further calibration before they can be used as rigorous prediction intervals.

summary:
