The closed set of MHD equations can be implemented in numerical codes to explore nonlinear effects during protostellar collapse, such as turbulence, angular momentum transport, and magnetic dust clumping.

title: A $C^2$-Perturbative Bernstein Theorem for Anisotropic Entire Minimal Graphs
comment: We solve the $C^{2}$ entire-graph version of the anisotropic Bernstein problem posed by Mooney-Yang \cite{MooneyYang2024} by proving that, for $1\le n\le 7$, entire smooth solutions $u$ of $Φ$-anisotropic minimal hypersurfaces equation are linear functions provided the anisotropic integrand is sufficiently $C^{2}$--close to the classical area functional
summary: We prove a Bernstein theorem for $Φ$-anisotropic minimal hypersurfaces in dimensions $1\leq n\leq 7$ that the only entire smooth solutions $u$ of $Φ$-anisotropic minimal hypersurfaces equation are affine functions provided the anisotropic area functional integrand $Φ$ is sufficiently $C^{2}$--close to the Euclidean area integrand. This settles the $C^2$ entire--graph version of anisotropic Bernstein problem posed by Mooney and Yang \cite{MooneyYang2024}, and the proof uses a compactness--rigidity argument combined with Figalli's regularity theorem established in \cite{Figalli2017}.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a Bernstein theorem for Φ-anisotropic minimal hypersurfaces in dimensions 1≤n≤7, showing that entire smooth solutions to the anisotropic minimal hypersurface equation are affine functions when the anisotropic integrand Φ is sufficiently C²-close to the Euclidean area integrand.
AI.motivation: The work resolves the C² entire-graph version of the anisotropic Bernstein problem posed by Mooney and Yang, extending classical Bernstein theorems to the anisotropic setting.
AI.method: The proof employs a compactness-rigidity argument combined with Figalli's regularity theorem.
AI.result: Establishes that the only entire smooth solutions in dimensions 1≤n≤7 are affine functions, provided Φ is sufficiently C²-close to the Euclidean integrand.
AI.conclusion: Settles the C² entire-graph version of the anisotropic Bernstein problem posed by Mooney and Yang.

title: Convergence analysis of Parametric Probabilistic Manifold Decomposition
summary:
This paper presents a convergence analysis for a newly developed nonlinear model reduction method: parametric probabilistic manifold decomposition (PPMD)~\cite{guo2026parametric}. In addition, existing analyzes of nonlinear reduced order models typically treat subspace reduction, manifold representation, regression, and nonlinear reconstruction as separate components and often remain at the level of discrete state vectors. To the best of our knowledge, no theory tracks the complete error propagation in a data-dependent model whose basis, residual geometry, spectral coordinates, parameter maps, and lifting operator are all learned from the same numerical solution data.
  We develop a coupled perturbation analysis for the entire PPMD procedure. A trajectory geometry induced by the spatial discretization and temporal quadrature connects discrete trajectory vectors isometrically with the corresponding PDE norm. Population spectral objects are introduced to align the empirical residual coordinates and derive a uniform coordinate error estimate, whose propagation through the Hilbert-valued kernel lifting estimator is then quantified. Combining these results with the full order discretization error, weighted low-rank approximation, parameter regression, and residual representation defect yields deterministic and high-probability trajectory error bounds and consistency in probability in the continuous PDE trajectory space. The theory identifies how the principal errors interact and which components limit the accuracy of the nonlinear reduced order model.

AI.tldr: This paper provides the first comprehensive convergence and error propagation analysis for Parametric Probabilistic Manifold Decomposition (PPMD), a nonlinear model reduction method, tracking errors end-to-end through basis construction, spectral coordinates, parameter maps, and lifting operators—all learned from the same data—and establishes deterministic and high-probability error bounds in the continuous PDE trajectory space.
AI.motivation: Existing analyses of nonlinear reduced order models treat subspace reduction, manifold representation, regression, and nonlinear reconstruction as separate components and typically only work at the discrete state vector level. No prior theory tracks the complete error propagation in a data-dependent model where all components are learned from the same numerical solution data.
AI.method: The paper develops a coupled perturbation analysis for the entire PPMD procedure. It introduces a trajectory geometry induced by spatial discretization and temporal quadrature to connect discrete trajectories isometrically to PDE norms. Population spectral objects are used to align empirical residual coordinates and derive uniform coordinate error estimates, which are then propagated through a Hilbert-valued kernel lifting estimator. These results are combined with full order discretization error, weighted low-rank approximation, parameter regression, and residual representation defects.
AI.result: The analysis yields deterministic and high-probability trajectory error bounds, as well as consistency in probability in the continuous PDE trajectory space. The theory identifies how principal errors interact and which components limit the accuracy of the nonlinear reduced order model.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides a complete end-to-end theoretical foundation for PPMD, identifying the dominant error sources and their interactions, thereby enabling principled understanding and improvement of nonlinear reduced order models.

title: Saha's ionization in the Schwarzschild spacetime
summary: We investigate the Saha ionization equilibrium in the exterior Schwarzschild spacetime. Starting from the mass-shell condition for a massive particle, we derive the conserved energy associated with the timelike Killing symmetry and obtain its nonrelativistic limit in terms of the Schwarzschild lapse function. This energy is then incorporated into the Maxwell--Boltzmann distribution to construct the ionization balance as seen by an asymptotic observer. We show that the gravitational field modifies the Saha relation through the redshift of both the particle energies and the thermodynamic variables. By imposing the Tolman--Ehrenfest and Klein equilibrium conditions, the formulation expressed entirely in terms of locally measured quantities reduces to the standard flat-spacetime Saha equation. We further analyze the gravitational redshift of the ionization energy, the relative departure from the flat-spacetime ionization ratio, and the corresponding shift of the ionization fraction as a function of the asymptotic temperature. We also present the relativistic classical counterpart based on the Maxwell--Jüttner distribution and show explicitly that its leading correction is negligible in the temperature range where neutral hydrogen is appreciably abundant. These results provide a consistent description of ionization equilibrium in a static gravitational field and clarify the distinction between gravitational redshift effects and intrinsic modifications of local atomic physics.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates the Saha ionization equilibrium in exterior Schwarzschild spacetime, deriving the ionization balance as seen by an asymptotic observer, showing gravitational field modifies the Saha relation via redshift effects, and demonstrating that in locally measured quantities it reduces to the standard flat-spacetime equation.
AI.motivation: To provide a consistent description of ionization equilibrium in a static gravitational field and clarify the distinction between gravitational redshift effects and intrinsic modifications of local atomic physics.
AI.method: Derives the conserved energy from the timelike Killing symmetry via the mass-shell condition, obtains its nonrelativistic limit using the Schwarzschild lapse function, and incorporates this energy into the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. The formulation uses Tolman-Ehrenfest and Klein equilibrium conditions, and also presents a relativistic classical counterpart based on the Maxwell-Jüttner distribution.
AI.result: The gravitational field modifies the Saha relation through redshift of particle energies and thermodynamic variables. When expressed in locally measured quantities with Tolman-Ehrenfest and Klein conditions, it reduces to the standard flat-spacetime Saha equation. The leading relativistic correction from the Maxwell-Jüttner distribution is negligible in the temperature range where neutral hydrogen is appreciably abundant.
AI.conclusion: The results provide a consistent description of ionization equilibrium in a static gravitational field, distinguishing gravitational redshift effects from intrinsic local atomic physics modifications.

title: uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in a slab
summary: In this paper, we investigate the uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in a slab domain with no-slip boundary conditions. Specifically, under the given external force and the small Poiseuille flow assumptions, we prove that there is an H1 solution, and obtain the pointwise decay around the Poiseuille flow at far field. Furthermore, if the force is small, the solution is shown to be unique. The key point of the proof is the estimate of the Dirichlet integral of the solutions in the truncated domains and the Stokes regularity estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper studies the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in a slab domain with no-slip boundary conditions, proving the existence of an H1 solution under small Poiseuille flow assumptions, establishing pointwise decay around the Poiseuille flow at far field, and demonstrating uniqueness when the external force is small.
AI.motivation: The authors aim to understand the uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of stationary solutions to the Navier-Stokes equations in slab domains, which are important for applications such as pipe and channel flows. Understanding the behavior around Poiseuille flow in such settings is a fundamental question in fluid dynamics.
AI.method: The proof relies on two key technical ingredients: (1) estimating the Dirichlet integral of solutions in truncated domains, and (2) using Stokes regularity estimates. These tools are combined to establish existence, pointwise decay rates, and uniqueness of the H1 solution.
AI.result: The paper proves: (1) existence of an H1 solution under given external force and small Poiseuille flow assumptions, (2) pointwise decay of the solution around the Poiseuille flow at far field, and (3) uniqueness of the solution when the external force is sufficiently small.
AI.conclusion: The authors successfully establish existence, decay estimates, and uniqueness for stationary Navier-Stokes solutions in slab domains with no-slip boundaries, providing a complete picture of the solution behavior around Poiseuille flow under smallness assumptions.

title: Entropy-Stable and Physical-Constraint-Preserving DGSEM for Symmetry-Reduced General-Relativistic Hydrodynamics on Stationary Spacetimes
summary:
We develop an entropy-stable and physical-constraint-preserving discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method for symmetry-reduced general-relativistic hydrodynamics on prescribed stationary spacetimes. Using a local orthonormal transformation, the fluid variables are expressed in a form for which the relativistic hydrodynamic algebra and the admissible set are independent of the spatial metric, while the spacetime geometry enters through stationary coefficients. This separation allows entropy-conservative special-relativistic fluxes to be combined with a compatible discretization of the geometric source terms. On affine tensor-product meshes, the resulting DGSEM is conservative and satisfies a semidiscrete entropy inequality, while the transformed variables provide a convex framework for physical-constraint preservation.
  For practical stabilization, we use a geometry-only causal speed that is sufficient for both classical local Lax--Friedrichs entropy dissipation and the physical-constraint-preserving Lax--Friedrichs splitting. The fully discrete method combines this stabilization with SSP Runge--Kutta time stepping, oscillation elimination, and conservative local-orthonormal-state scaling. Numerical experiments cover smooth and strongly shocked special-relativistic flows, an axisymmetric jet, stationary Michel accretion, Schwarzschild Bondi--Hoyle flow, and four Kerr accretion cases. The results demonstrate the designed high-order accuracy in smooth regimes and robust performance for demanding relativistic flows on curved stationary backgrounds.

AI.tldr: An entropy-stable and physical-constraint-preserving discontinuous Galerkin spectral element method (DGSEM) is developed for symmetry-reduced general-relativistic hydrodynamics on stationary spacetimes. The method uses local orthonormal transformations to decouple fluid algebra from the spatial metric, enabling entropy-conservative fluxes, conservative discretization, semidiscrete entropy inequality, and physical-constraint preservation, validated through extensive tests including Kerr accretion flows.
AI.motivation: To develop a robust high-order numerical method for general-relativistic hydrodynamics that simultaneously guarantees entropy stability and physical-constraint preservation (e.g., positivity of density and pressure) on curved stationary spacetimes, which is challenging due to spacetime geometry coupling with the fluid evolution equations.
AI.method: The method applies a local orthonormal transformation to express fluid variables such that relativistic hydrodynamic algebra and admissible sets become independent of the spatial metric, with geometry entering only through stationary coefficients. This enables combining entropy-conservative special-relativistic fluxes with a compatible geometric source term discretization on affine tensor-product meshes. Stabilization uses a geometry-only causal speed for local Lax-Friedrichs entropy dissipation and physical-constraint-preserving Lax-Friedrichs splitting, integrated with SSP Runge-Kutta time stepping, oscillation elimination, and conservative local-orthonormal-state scaling.
AI.result: Numerical experiments across smooth and strongly shocked special-relativistic flows, an axisymmetric jet, stationary Michel accretion, Schwarzschild Bondi-Hoyle flow, and four Kerr accretion cases demonstrate designed high-order accuracy in smooth regimes and robust performance for demanding relativistic flows on curved stationary backgrounds.
AI.conclusion: The proposed DGSEM achieves simultaneous entropy stability and physical-constraint preservation for symmetry-reduced general-relativistic hydrodynamics on stationary spacetimes, verified through comprehensive numerical tests on both special- and general-relativistic configurations including black hole accretion scenarios.

title: D-RADI: A Low-rank ADI Algorithm for Solving Large-scale Discrete-time Algebraic Riccati Equations
summary: The low-rank alternating direction implicit (ADI) method is an efficient numerical technique for solving several types of large-scale matrix equations that admit low-rank solutions. The discrete-time algebraic Riccati equation (DARE) is an important matrix equation with applications in state estimation, controller design, and filter design. In the literature, the low-rank Cholesky factor ADI method for Stein equations has been used within Newton iterations to solve large-scale DAREs. However, no dedicated low-rank ADI solver is available for such DAREs. To address this gap, this paper presents a low-rank ADI solver for large-scale DAREs. We also propose an efficient approach to generate ADI shifts automatically, which makes the proposed solver fully autonomous for solving DAREs. The effectiveness of the proposed solver is compared with MATLAB's \texttt{idare} on a moderate-order problem. Efficiency and accuracy are further demonstrated on large-scale DAREs of order $10^6$. Numerical results confirm that the solver is efficient, accurate, and fully autonomous.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first dedicated low-rank ADI solver for large-scale discrete-time algebraic Riccati equations (DAREs), including an automatic approach for generating ADI shifts, making the solver fully autonomous. It is validated against MATLAB's idare on moderate-order problems and demonstrates efficiency and accuracy on DAREs of order 10^6.
AI.motivation: The low-rank ADI method is efficient for large-scale matrix equations with low-rank solutions, and DAREs are important in state estimation, controller design, and filter design. While low-rank Cholesky factor ADI for Stein equations has been used inside Newton iterations for DAREs, no dedicated low-rank ADI solver exists specifically for DAREs, creating a gap the paper aims to fill.
AI.method: The paper develops a low-rank ADI solver specifically tailored for large-scale DAREs. It also introduces an efficient automatic strategy for generating ADI shifts, eliminating the need for manual tuning and making the solver fully autonomous for DARE solving.
AI.result: The proposed solver is compared with MATLAB's idare on a moderate-order problem. Efficiency and accuracy are further demonstrated on large-scale DAREs of order 10^6, with numerical results confirming the solver is efficient, accurate, and fully autonomous.
AI.conclusion: The dedicated low-rank ADI solver with automatic shift generation successfully addresses the gap in the literature, providing an efficient, accurate, and fully autonomous numerical method for solving large-scale DAREs.

title: Exact Rayleigh Reduction for Direct Detection of Turning Bifurcations
summary:
We introduce an exact Rayleigh reduction for the direct construction and detection of turning bifurcations in nonlinear parameter-dependent equations. A generalized Rayleigh functional ordinarily provides only a scalar necessary constraint on solutions. We show that, along a suitable one-parameter transformation orbit $u=\mathcal G_sφ$, it can instead become the exact parameter law $λ=\mathcal R(\mathcal G_sφ)$ of a genuine solution branch. Turning points are then found from nondegenerate critical points of this one-dimensional Rayleigh profile. The branch tangent automatically yields a kernel direction of the state linearization, and under the usual Fredholm, kernel-simplicity, and parameter-transversality assumptions the detected point is a simple fold.
  For Kirchhoff equations, amplitude scaling on bounded domains and spatial dilation on $\mathbb R^N$ yield explicit exact branches, global parameter thresholds, and countable hierarchies of turning values. For the generalized Kirchhoff law $M_b(A)=a+bA^θ$, the branch geometry is governed by the dimension--homogeneity index $θ(N-2)-2$: an interior turning bifurcation occurs exactly when $θ(N-2)>2$. This gives a universal bifurcation trichotomy that is independent of the particular Berestycki--Lions nonlinearity.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an exact Rayleigh reduction method for directly constructing and detecting turning bifurcations in nonlinear parameter-dependent equations, demonstrating that a generalized Rayleigh functional can become an exact parameter law along a one-parameter transformation orbit. The method is applied to Kirchhoff equations, revealing a universal bifurcation trichotomy governed by the dimension-homogeneity index θ(N−2)−2.
AI.motivation: Turning bifurcations (folds) in nonlinear parameter-dependent equations are typically difficult to detect; previous approaches using generalized Rayleigh functionals only provide scalar necessary constraints rather than exact parameter relationships, limiting their utility for direct bifurcation analysis.
AI.method: The authors show that along a suitable one-parameter transformation orbit u = G_s φ, the generalized Rayleigh functional becomes the exact parameter law λ = R(G_s φ) for a genuine solution branch. Turning points are identified from nondegenerate critical points of this one-dimensional profile, with the branch tangent providing a kernel direction of the state linearization. This is applied to Kirchhoff equations via amplitude scaling (bounded domains) and spatial dilation (R^N).
AI.result: For Kirchhoff equations with the generalized law M_b(A)=a+bA^θ, the branch geometry is governed by the dimension-homogeneity index θ(N−2)−2: an interior turning bifurcation occurs exactly when θ(N−2)>2. This yields a universal bifurcation trichotomy independent of the specific Berestycki–Lions nonlinearity, along with explicit global parameter thresholds and countable hierarchies of turning values.
AI.conclusion: The exact Rayleigh reduction provides a rigorous framework for constructing and detecting turning points, with the Kirchhoff application revealing a structure-dependent yet nonlinearity-independent bifurcation trichotomy. Under standard Fredholm, kernel-simplicity, and parameter-transversality assumptions, the detected points are confirmed as simple folds.

title: A Spectral Identifiability Threshold for Dissipative Rate Recovery from Truncated Liouvillian Spectra
comment: 15 pages, 6 figures. Data and code are available at Zenodo, DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.22160077
summary: Open quantum systems lose energy and phase coherence through different dissipative processes, but these processes can produce overlapping dynamical signatures. The Liouvillian spectrum summarizes how such a system relaxes, yet it is not obvious how much of that spectrum is needed to distinguish the underlying dissipation rates. We study this question for amplitude damping and dephasing in a six-qubit Lindblad model whose spectrum can be derived analytically. We retain only the slowest non-steady spectral modes and ask how many are required before each dissipative rate becomes recoverable. We show that population modes contain no dephasing information, which creates a lower bound of D = 2^n retained modes for uniform dephasing identifiability in the relevant rate regime. The measured recovery threshold reaches this bound at n = 4,5,6, while n = 3 remains above it. At n = 6, least squares achieves a mean joint absolute error of order 10^-9, compared with 4.355 x 10^-4 for four tabular learning methods. Robustness tests show that this advantage weakens when the spectra are perturbed and when a transverse field breaks the commuting structure. These results show that the amount and structure of retained spectral information can determine whether dissipative parameters are recoverable, independently of the estimator used. The present conclusions apply to noise-free simulator spectra rather than measurement-derived spectra.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how many of the slowest Liouvillian spectral modes are needed to identify amplitude damping and dephasing rates in a six-qubit Lindblad system. It finds a fundamental lower bound of D=2^n modes for dephasing identifiability, demonstrates that least squares achieves near machine-precision recovery at n=6 (far outperforming tabular learning methods), and shows that this advantage degrades under spectral perturbations and symmetry-breaking fields.
AI.motivation: Different dissipative processes (amplitude damping vs. dephasing) in open quantum systems can produce overlapping dynamical signatures, making it unclear how much of the Liouvillian spectrum is needed to distinguish underlying dissipation rates. This question of identifiability of dissipative parameters from limited spectral information has not been systematically characterized.
AI.method: The authors study a six-qubit Lindblad model with amplitude damping and dephasing whose Liouvillian spectrum is analytically derivable. They retain only the slowest non-steady spectral modes and systematically determine how many are required before each dissipative rate becomes recoverable, comparing least squares optimization against tabular learning methods.
AI.result: Population modes contain no dephasing information, establishing a lower bound of D=2^n retained modes for uniform dephasing identifiability. The measured recovery threshold reaches this bound at n=4,5,6, but n=3 remains above it. At n=6, least squares achieves mean joint absolute error ~10^-9 versus ~4.355x10^-4 for four tabular learning methods. This advantage weakens under spectral perturbations and when a transverse field breaks commutativity.
AI.conclusion: The amount and structure of retained spectral information determines whether dissipative parameters are recoverable, independently of the estimator used. The conclusions apply to noise-free simulator spectra rather than measurement-derived spectra, and reveal fundamental information-theoretic limits on parameter identifiability in open quantum systems.

title: A Tensor Neural Network Method for High-Order Homogenization of Locally Periodic Elliptic Problems
summary: We develop a high-order tensor neural network (TNN) method for locally periodic elliptic multiscale problems of the form $-\nabla\cdot(A(x,x/\varepsilon)\nabla u_\varepsilon)=f$. Because the coefficient depends on both the slow variable $x$ and the fast periodic variable $y=x/\varepsilon$, the high-order cell problems and macroscopic corrector equations are more involved than in the classical case $A=A(y)$, and the correctors depend parametrically on $x$. We derive a computable high-order two-scale expansion and prove an $H^1$ convergence estimate for the partial expansion in boundary-layer-free settings, including periodic domains and ideal boundary-matching configurations. The proof uses the recursive compatibility structure of the corrector hierarchy and a zero-mean oscillation estimate in $H^{-1}$. We then construct a TNN framework for the high-dimensional corrector problems. Its tensor-product structure permits deterministic one-dimensional quadrature for the cell problems, homogenized coefficients, macroscopic source terms, and loss functions, avoiding Monte Carlo integration error. The numerical realization assumes that the coefficient entries and assembled data admit finite or controlled tensor-product representations; this computational assumption is separate from the general matrix-valued coefficient class used in the analysis. Experiments with scalar locally periodic coefficients show accurate high-order correctors. The $H^1$ semi-norm errors are consistent with the proved estimate, while point-normalized $L^2$ errors display the nominal high-order behavior predicted by the formal expansion.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a high-order tensor neural network (TNN) method for locally periodic elliptic multiscale problems, deriving computable high-order two-scale expansions with H^1 convergence guarantees and demonstrating accurate high-order correctors in numerical experiments.
AI.motivation: Locally periodic multiscale problems (where coefficients depend on both slow and fast variables) yield more complex high-order cell problems and macroscopic corrector equations than classical periodic settings, with parametric dependence of correctors on x. This requires new computational methods.
AI.method: Derives computable high-order two-scale expansions with proofs of H^1 convergence using recursive compatibility structure and zero-mean oscillation estimates in H^{-1}. Constructs a tensor neural network framework for high-dimensional corrector problems, leveraging tensor-product structure for deterministic one-dimensional quadrature (avoiding Monte Carlo error).
AI.result: Numerical experiments with scalar locally periodic coefficients show accurate high-order correctors. H^1 semi-norm errors are consistent with the proved estimate, and point-normalized L^2 errors display the nominal high-order behavior predicted by the formal expansion.
AI.conclusion: The TNN method provides an effective computational framework for high-order correctors in locally periodic multiscale problems, with rigorous convergence guarantees in boundary-layer-free settings and practical numerical accuracy at high orders.

title: Apriori Estimates and Nonexistence Results for Some Quasilinear Problems in a Half-Space
summary: We obtain apriori estimates for positive solutions of some quasilinear elliptic problems in a half-space. Using these estimates and other techniques, we derive new nonexistence results for the respective Dirichlet problems.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes a priori estimates for positive solutions of quasilinear elliptic problems in a half-space and uses these estimates along with other techniques to derive new nonexistence results for the corresponding Dirichlet problems.
AI.motivation: To obtain new nonexistence results for quasilinear elliptic Dirichlet problems in a half-space, which requires first establishing a priori estimates for positive solutions of these problems.
AI.method: The authors derive a priori estimates for positive solutions of quasilinear elliptic problems in a half-space, then combine these estimates with other analytical techniques to prove nonexistence results for the Dirichlet problems.
AI.result: New nonexistence results for the Dirichlet problems in a half-space are derived, built upon the newly obtained a priori estimates.
AI.conclusion: The a priori estimates obtained serve as a foundation for proving new nonexistence results for quasilinear elliptic Dirichlet problems in a half-space.

title: Advancing Lead-Free FASnI3 Perovskite Solar Cells via Cu-Doped NiOx HTL Engineering: An Optoelectronic Analysis
summary: Efficient lead-free perovskite solar cells remain limited by inefficient charge transport and significant recombination losses. In this work, copper (Cu) doped nickel oxide (NiOx) is employed as the hole transport layer (HTL) in a formamidinium tin iodide (FASnI3) perovskite solar cell to improve hole extraction and suppress carrier losses. The optoelectronic response of the proposed device architecture is evaluated through a coupled numerical framework combining finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) optical simulations with finite element method (FEM)-based electrical modeling. Electrical analysis solves the Poisson equation together with the drift-diffusion and carrier continuity equations, while accounting for radiative, non-adiative, and interfacial recombination mechanisms. Systematic optimization of the thicknesses and doping concentrations of the constituent layers was performed to establish a high-performance device configuration. Following optimization of layer dimensions and carrier densities, the device achieved a power conversion efficiency (PCE) of 24.71%. Integrating an anti-reflection coating (ARC) effectively suppressed reflection losses, yielding a 5.47% relative enhancement in PCE. Consequently, the optimized device achieved a peak PCE of 26.06%, with a short-circuit current density (Jsc) of 28.98 mA/cm2, an open-circuit voltage (Voc) of 1.051 V, and a fill factor (FF) of 85.64%. These findings demonstrate that Cu-doped NiOx functions as a highly promising HTL to boost charge collection and maximize overall efficiency in lead-free FASnI3 solar cells.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a numerical study of a lead-free FASnI3 perovskite solar cell employing Cu-doped NiOx as the hole transport layer, achieving a peak PCE of 26.06% through coupled FDTD optical and FEM electrical simulations, with systematic optimization of layer thicknesses/doping and anti-reflection coating integration.
AI.motivation: Lead-free perovskite solar cells suffer from inefficient charge transport and high recombination losses. There is a need to improve hole extraction and suppress carrier losses in tin-based (FASnI3) perovskite solar cells to achieve higher efficiency without toxic lead.
AI.method: Coupled numerical framework combining FDTD optical simulations with FEM-based electrical modeling. Electrical analysis solves the Poisson equation, drift-diffusion and carrier continuity equations, accounting for radiative, non-radiative, and interfacial recombination mechanisms. Systematic optimization of layer thicknesses and doping concentrations was performed, and an anti-reflection coating (ARC) was integrated to suppress reflection losses.
AI.result: The optimized device achieved a PCE of 24.71% before ARC integration. Adding the ARC yielded a 5.47% relative PCE enhancement, resulting in a peak PCE of 26.06%, with Jsc of 28.98 mA/cm2, Voc of 1.051 V, and FF of 85.64%.
AI.conclusion: Cu-doped NiOx serves as a highly promising HTL for boosting charge collection and maximizing overall efficiency in lead-free FASnI3 solar cells, demonstrating the viability of efficient lead-free perovskite photovoltaics.

title: Two-point modulus for the logarithmic p-flux of the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the p-Laplacian
summary:
We study two-point estimates for the logarithmic \(p\)-flux \[ X_Ω:= |
abla\log u|^{p-2}
abla\log u, \] where \(u\) is the positive first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the \(p\)-Laplacian on a bounded convex domain \(Ω\). When \(p=2\), this reduces to \(
abla\log u\), whose sharp modulus of concavity is a key ingredient in the proof of the fundamental gap conjecture by Andrews and Clutterbuck. We investigate whether an analogous one-dimensional modulus persists for \(p
eq2\). We first prove sharp two-point estimates on intervals and balls for every \(p>1\). On balls, the sharp radial modulus is strictly larger than the corresponding one-dimensional modulus. In contrast, in dimensions \(N\ge2\), the one-dimensional modulus fails in general on convex domains for every \(p
eq2\). For \(1<p<2\), the counterexample is obtained from the boundary behavior near a flat portion of the boundary and is preserved under smooth convex approximation. For \(p>2\), we use thin rectangles and derive the limiting behavior \(u_\varepsilon(x,0)ightarrow(\cosπx)^{2/p}\), together with a second-order expansion of the rescaled first eigenvalue. Finally, we decompose the symmetric derivative of the nonlinear logarithmic flux relative to the level sets of \(-\log u\). The decomposition shows how the tangential variation of \(|

AI.tldr: This paper studies two-point estimates for the logarithmic p-flux X_Ω of the first Dirichlet eigenfunction of the p-Laplacian on convex domains. The authors prove sharp estimates on intervals and balls for all p>1, show the one-dimensional modulus fails in higher dimensions for p≠2 (with counterexamples via flat boundary behavior for 1<p<2 and thin rectangles for p>2), and decompose the symmetric derivative of the nonlinear flux to explain the special roles of p=2, one dimension, and radial symmetry.
AI.motivation: When p=2, the sharp modulus of concavity of ∇log u is a key ingredient in the proof of the fundamental gap conjecture by Andrews and Clutterbuck. This raises the question of whether an analogous one-dimensional modulus persists for p≠2, which is investigated here.
AI.method: The paper proves sharp two-point estimates on intervals and balls for every p>1, constructs counterexamples showing failure of the one-dimensional modulus in dimensions N≥2 for p≠2 (using boundary behavior near flat portions for 1<p<2 and thin rectangles with limiting behavior u_ε→(cosπx)^{2/p} for p>2), and decomposes the symmetric derivative of the nonlinear logarithmic flux relative to level sets.

AI.conclusion: The decomposition shows how tangential variation of |∇log u| separates log-concavity from monotonicity of the nonlinear flux, and explains the special roles of p=2, one dimension, and radial symmetry.

title: Elastic properties of amorphous LiTaCl$_6$ solid-state electrolyte
summary: Amorphous solid-state electrolytes are attractive candidates for safe, high-energy-density all-solid-state batteries, yet their mechanical properties remain poorly understood from a computational perspective. Here, we investigate the elastic behavior of the recently discovered amorphous superionic Li-ion conductor LiTaCl$_6$ using density-functional-theory (DFT)-based methods, including unrelaxed static, relaxed static, and strain fluctuations from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations in the isobaric--isothermal (NPT) ensemble with DFT-trained machine-learning force fields (MLFFs). While the unrelaxed static method predicts a Young's modulus an order of magnitude higher than the experiment, the relaxed static method---commonly applied to crystalline electrolytes---still overestimates the modulus by more than 170%. In contrast, the MD approach using MLFFs yields a Young's modulus of $2.84 \pm 0.26$ GPa, which quantitatively agrees with the experimental value of $2.91 \pm 0.32$ GPa. Using the MLFF-MD approach, we further predict bulk modulus (4.44 GPa), shear modulus (1.02 GPa), and Poisson's ratio (0.39) for amorphous LiTaCl$_6$ and conclude that elastically it behaves like a soft polymer or gel. These results demonstrate that amorphous superionic materials possess some unique elastic properties and that, among the methods examined, only the MLFF-MD approach yields quantitative agreement with experiment, highlighting the necessity of a dynamical treatment to simulate their elastic response, consistent with recent findings for crystalline superionic conductors.

AI.tldr: This paper computationally investigates the elastic properties of amorphous LiTaCl6, a superionic Li-ion conductor, using DFT-based methods. While static methods (unrelaxed and relaxed) significantly overestimate Young's modulus, a machine-learning force field (MLFF) driven molecular dynamics approach in the NPT ensemble quantitatively matches experiment (2.84 vs 2.91 GPa), revealing that amorphous superionic conductors behave like soft polymers/gels and require dynamical treatment to correctly capture their elastic response.
AI.motivation: Amorphous solid-state electrolytes are promising for safe, high-energy-density all-solid-state batteries, but their mechanical properties remain poorly understood computationally. Accurate prediction of elastic behavior is essential for practical battery design.
AI.method: The authors use three DFT-based approaches: (1) unrelaxed static method, (2) relaxed static method (commonly applied to crystalline electrolytes), and (3) molecular dynamics simulations in the NPT ensemble using DFT-trained machine-learning force fields, analyzing strain fluctuations to extract elastic moduli.
AI.result: The unrelaxed static method overestimates Young's modulus by an order of magnitude, and the relaxed static method overestimates by >170%. The MLFF-MD approach yields Young's modulus of 2.84±0.26 GPa, quantitatively matching the experimental 2.91±0.32 GPa. Additional predicted properties: bulk modulus 4.44 GPa, shear modulus 1.02 GPa, Poisson's ratio 0.39, indicating gel-like elastic behavior.
AI.conclusion: Amorphous superionic materials possess unique elastic properties (soft polymer/gel-like behavior), and only the MLFF-MD dynamical approach yields quantitative agreement with experiment, highlighting the necessity of dynamical treatment for simulating their elastic response—consistent with recent findings for crystalline superionic conductors.

title: Dynamic subscales and unconditional semi-discrete stability for non-residual VMS approximations of generalised Newtonian flows
summary: We analyse a non-residual variational multiscale finite element formulation with dynamic subscales for incompressible generalised Newtonian Navier--Stokes flows. The apparent viscosity is assumed to be bounded and Lipschitz continuous with respect to the shear rate, covering several regularised rheological laws. The method separates, through orthogonal projections, the unresolved pressure-divergence, convective, and pressure-gradient contributions. For the linearised semi-discrete problem, we prove well-posedness and an unconditional stability estimate in an anisotropic VMS norm. The estimate controls viscous dissipation, subscale energies, discrete divergence, and a coupled acceleration-convection-pressure balance. For the non-linear formulation, a fixed-point argument yields existence and optimal-order a priori bounds under suitable regularity and smallness assumptions. The analysis also provides weak-in-time control of the discrete pressure-convection balance. A key point is that the dynamic pressure-related subscale provides the time-derivative contribution needed to control the projected pressure-gradient error, a mechanism unavailable in the corresponding quasi-static setting.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a non-residual variational multiscale finite element method with dynamic subscales for incompressible generalized Newtonian Navier-Stokes flows, proving well-posedness, unconditional stability, and optimal-order error bounds for both linearized and nonlinear formulations.
AI.motivation: To provide rigorous mathematical analysis of a variational multiscale method with dynamic subscales for generalized Newtonian flows, addressing the gap in stability and convergence theory for such formulations where the dynamic pressure-related subscale plays a crucial role that the quasi-static setting cannot offer.
AI.method: The method separates unresolved pressure-divergence, convective, and pressure-gradient contributions through orthogonal projections within a variational multiscale framework. Analysis uses anisotropic VMS norms, well-posedness theory for linearized semi-discrete problems, and fixed-point arguments for the nonlinear case.
AI.result: Unconditional stability in anisotropic VMS norm controlling viscous dissipation, subscale energies, discrete divergence, and acceleration-convection-pressure balance; existence and optimal-order a priori error bounds for the nonlinear formulation; weak-in-time control of discrete pressure-convection balance.
AI.conclusion: The dynamic pressure-related subscale provides the time-derivative contribution essential for controlling the projected pressure-gradient error, a mechanism unavailable in quasi-static settings, making the dynamic subscale formulation theoretically superior.

title: Stable $C^{7/9}$ cusp formation for the Novikov equation
summary: We establish stable cusp formation for the Novikov equation, a cubically nonlinear Camassa--Holm-type equation. We identify an open set of smooth initial data for which the first gradient blow-up produces a cusp with sharp Hölder regularity $C^{7/9}$. This result shows that, in nonlocal wave-breaking problems, the sharp regularity of the cusp is not determined by the nonlocal or nonlinear structure alone. While the conserved $H^1$-type quantity excludes the $C^{1/3}$ cusp associated with Burgers-type gradient blow-up, the precise Hölder exponent is selected by the coupling between the nonlocal term and the algebraic structure of the nonlinearity. In the Novikov equation, this coupling yields the exponent $7/9$, rather than the $3/5$ exponent known for the Camassa--Holm and Hunter--Saxton equations. The main difficulty is that the naive high-frequency limit retains the cubic character of the equation and therefore does not exhibit a self-similar leading flow. We overcome this by introducing a Galilean-type change of variables around a nonzero background, which reveals a quadratic Hunter--Saxton-type leading equation. Its self-similar profiles determine the $C^{7/9}$ cusp, while the nonlocal and cubic remainders are controlled perturbatively in modulated similarity variables.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes stable cusp formation for the Novikov equation, showing that first gradient blow-up produces a cusp with sharp Hölder regularity C^{7/9}. This is achieved via a Galilean-type change of variables that reveals a quadratic Hunter-Saxton-type leading equation, whose self-similar profiles determine the cusp exponent.
AI.motivation: To understand how sharp regularity of cusps in nonlocal wave-breaking problems is determined—specifically whether it depends on the nonlocal/nonlinear structure alone—and to determine the precise Hölder exponent for the Novikov equation (a cubically nonlinear Camassa-Holm-type equation), which was unknown.
AI.method: The authors identify an open set of smooth initial data leading to gradient blow-up. They overcome the difficulty that the naive high-frequency limit retains cubic character (lacking self-similar leading flow) by introducing a Galilean-type change of variables around a nonzero background, which reveals a quadratic Hunter-Saxton-type leading equation. The self-similar profiles of this equation determine the C^{7/9} cusp, and nonlocal/cubic remainders are controlled perturbatively in modulated similarity variables.
AI.result: Stable cusp formation is established for the Novikov equation with sharp Hölder regularity C^{7/9} for the first gradient blow-up, contrasting with the C^{1/3} Burgers-type cusp (excluded by conserved H^1-type quantity) and the 3/5 exponent for Camassa-Holm and Hunter-Saxton equations.
AI.conclusion: The sharp Hölder exponent of cusp formation is not determined by the nonlocal or nonlinear structure alone, but is selected by the coupling between the nonlocal term and the algebraic structure of the nonlinearity. For the Novikov equation this yields 7/9, distinct from the 3/5 for Camassa-Holm/Hunter-Saxton.

title: ENPINN: Energy-Norm-Guided Gradient-Enhanced PINNs for Generalized Transport Problems with Sharp Gradients
summary: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) have emerged as a meshless alternative to conventional numerical methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs). However, their limited ability to capture sharp gradients can lead to substantial errors when resolving boundary and interior layers. Here, we introduce an energy-norm-enhanced PINN (ENPINN) that incorporates gradient information and variational structure into the loss function to improve the resolution of layer-dominated solutions. We first examine two related formulations: weak-loss PINNs (WLPINNs), which incorporate test functions into the conventional PINN residual, and gradient-enhanced PINNs (gPINNs), which augment the loss with spatial derivatives of the PDE residual. By analyzing these formulations, we identify their limitations in resolving steep solution gradients and motivate the systematic construction of ENPINN. We establish theoretically how the energy-norm error depends on the ENPINN loss and show that a suitably modified residual-derivative term is essential for accurately capturing boundary layers. We further establish the existence of neural-network approximations with arbitrarily small energy error and derive corresponding derivative bounds, providing a theoretical foundation for the proposed framework. The performance of ENPINN is assessed through systematic comparisons with existing PINN variants for convection-diffusion-reaction problems exhibiting steep gradients. Numerical experiments include a combustion model, a coupled multi-scale system, a two-dimensional Burgers equation with an interior layer, and a three-dimensional time-dependent problem.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an energy-norm-enhanced PINN (ENPINN) that incorporates gradient information and variational structure into the loss function to improve the resolution of layer-dominated solutions for PDEs.
AI.motivation: Standard PINNs struggle to capture sharp gradients, leading to substantial errors when resolving boundary and interior layers in PDE solutions. Existing variants (weak-loss PINNs and gradient-enhanced PINNs) have limitations in resolving steep solution gradients.
AI.method: The authors introduce ENPINN, which combines gradient information and variational structure into the loss function. They first analyze WLPINNs and gPINNs to identify their limitations, then systematically construct ENPINN. The paper establishes theoretical relationships between energy-norm error and the ENPINN loss, proves existence of neural-network approximations with arbitrarily small energy error, and derives derivative bounds.
AI.result: ENPINN is assessed through systematic comparisons with existing PINN variants on convection-diffusion-reaction problems with steep gradients, including a combustion model, a coupled multi-scale system, a 2D Burgers equation with an interior layer, and a 3D time-dependent problem.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides both theoretical foundations and numerical evidence that ENPINN, with its suitably modified residual-derivative term, is essential for accurately capturing boundary layers and achieving better resolution of layer-dominated solutions than existing PINN formulations.

title: Global Existence of classical solutions to 3D nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations with low-regularity initial data
summary: This paper studies global existence for the Cauchy problem of nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations in three space dimensions, strictly within the regularity regime of classical local existence. We prove it via higher-order and lower-order energy estimates. The proof relies on two key ingredients. The first is due to the work of Georgiev and Popivanov, which reduces quadratic nonlinearities to cubic terms plus ghost-energy-controllable terms, securing lower-order estimates. The second is a sharp Klainerman-Sobolev-type inequality without the scaling operator, established herein, which yields enough time decay for derivatives up to second order; integration by parts then controls derivative loss terms in the higher-order estimates.

AI.tldr: This paper proves global existence for the Cauchy problem of nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations in 3D, working strictly within the classical local existence regularity regime, using higher-order and lower-order energy estimates.
AI.motivation: To establish global existence for nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations in three space dimensions, even when the regularity is at the borderline of classical local existence—a regime not previously covered by existing global existence results.
AI.method: The proof combines two key ingredients: (1) the Georgiev-Popivanov reduction that converts quadratic nonlinearities into cubic terms plus ghost-energy-controllable terms (for lower-order estimates), and (2) a new sharp Klainerman-Sobolev-type inequality without the scaling operator that provides sufficient time decay for second-order derivatives, with integration by parts controlling derivative loss in higher-order estimates.
AI.result: Global existence is proven for the Cauchy problem of nonlinear Klein-Gordon equations in three space dimensions within the regularity regime of classical local existence.
AI.conclusion: The authors establish global solutions at the minimal regularity threshold using a novel combination of energy estimates and a scaling-free Klainerman-Sobolev inequality, extending the reach of classical global existence results.

title: Harnessing the skyrmion Hall effect for low-power skyrmion transport in a tubular synthetic antiferromagnet
summary: We show that optimal control can turn the skyrmion Hall effect from a source of typically unwanted transverse motion into a mechanism for reducing Ohmic losses in skyrmion transport. We consider a pair of antiferromagnetically coupled skyrmions confined to a tubular geometry, where their relative transverse displacement becomes a periodic internal coordinate. The skyrmion Hall effect drives this coordinate, while finite interlayer coupling makes the resulting relation between applied current and longitudinal velocity nonlinear, allowing different current protocols to produce the same prescribed average velocity. We determine which of these protocols minimizes Joule heating. Depending on the interlayer coupling and spin-transfer-torque parameters, the optimal current is either constant, with the skyrmion pair maintaining a fixed relative position, or time dependent, with the pair undergoing periodic relative motion around the tube. In either case, the additional internal degree of freedom created by the skyrmion Hall effect and interlayer coupling enables skyrmion transport at a lower power than in the uncoupled limit.

AI.tldr: This paper shows that the skyrmion Hall effect, typically a source of unwanted transverse motion, can be harnessed in antiferromagnetically coupled skyrmion pairs confined to a tubular geometry to reduce Ohmic losses during transport. The optimal current protocol (constant vs. time-dependent) that minimizes Joule heating depends on interlayer coupling and spin-transfer-torque parameters, but in all cases the coupled system achieves lower power transport than the uncoupled limit.
AI.motivation: The skyrmion Hall effect causes undesirable transverse motion in skyrmion transport, and minimizing energy dissipation (Ohmic losses) is important for practical skyrmion-based devices. This work explores whether this typically problematic effect can be repurposed to reduce power consumption.
AI.method: The authors consider a pair of antiferromagnetically coupled skyrmions in a tubular geometry where relative transverse displacement serves as a periodic internal coordinate. They use optimal control theory to determine current protocols that minimize Joule heating while achieving a prescribed average velocity, analyzing how the optimal solution depends on interlayer coupling and spin-transfer-torque parameters.
AI.result: The optimal current protocol is either constant (skyrmion pair maintains fixed relative position) or time-dependent (periodic relative motion around the tube), depending on system parameters. In both cases, the internal degree of freedom from the skyrmion Hall effect and interlayer coupling enables lower-power skyrmion transport compared to the uncoupled limit.
AI.conclusion: The skyrmion Hall effect, combined with interlayer coupling in a tubular geometry, creates an exploitable internal degree of freedom that can reduce Ohmic losses in skyrmion transport—transforming a typically detrimental effect into a mechanism for increased energy efficiency.

title: Analysis and Approximation of Stochastic Multiscale Subdiffusion Driven by Fractional Gaussian Noise
summary: This paper investigates a stochastic multiscale subdiffusion model driven by fractional Gaussian noise, where the multiscale Abel kernel with variable exponent $α(t)\in(0,1)$ is used to capture multiscale and crossover behavior in anomalous diffusion. The main difficulties of this model lie in the complexity of the multiscale Abel kernel (e.g. non-monotonicity and non-coercivity) and the low regularity caused by the noise. Concerning these issues, we prove the well-posedness and regularity of the mild solutions by means of solution operator approach and a perturbation technique for multiscale Abel kernel. Then both the semidiscrete-in-time and fully-discrete numerical schemes are proposed and analyzed under the low-regularity numerical analysis framework, with proved temporal and spatial convergence rates. Numerical experiments are presented to substantiate the theoretical results.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes a stochastic multiscale subdiffusion model with fractional Gaussian noise and a variable-exponent multiscale Abel kernel, proving well-posedness and regularity of mild solutions, and developing semidiscrete and fully-discrete numerical schemes with proven convergence rates.
AI.motivation: The model's complexity arises from the non-monotonic and non-coercive multiscale Abel kernel combined with low regularity induced by fractional Gaussian noise, making analysis challenging yet important for capturing multiscale and crossover behavior in anomalous diffusion.
AI.method: The authors employ a solution operator approach for well-posedness, a perturbation technique to handle the multiscale Abel kernel, and a low-regularity numerical analysis framework to analyze both semidiscrete-in-time and fully-discrete numerical schemes.
AI.result: Well-posedness and regularity of mild solutions are established, and both temporal and spatial convergence rates for the proposed numerical schemes are proven, with numerical experiments validating the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed theoretical and numerical frameworks successfully address the challenges of stochastic multiscale subdiffusion with variable-exponent Abel kernels, providing rigorous convergence guarantees under low regularity conditions.

title: Global small data radial symmetric solutions of 3D semilinear Euler-Poisson-Darboux equations
summary: For the 3D semilinear Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation $\square u+\fracμ{t}\partial_tu=|u|^p$, where $t\geq1$, $μ>0$ and $p>1$, it is conjectured that there is a critical exponent $p_{crit}(3,μ)=\max\{p_s(3+μ), p_f(3)\}$ with the Strauss exponent $p_s(3+μ)=\frac{μ+4+\sqrt{μ^2+16μ+32}}{2(μ+2)}$ and the Fujita exponent $p_f(3)=\frac{5}{3}$ such that when $p>p_{crit}(3,μ)$, the small data solution $u$ exists globally, otherwise, when $1<p\le p_{crit}(3,μ)$, the solution $u$ can blow up in finite time. It is pointed out that for $1<p\le p_{crit}(3,μ)$, the blowup of solution $u$ has been shown. However, it is still open for the global existence of small solution $u$ when $p>p_{crit}(3,μ)$. Note that $p_{crit}(3,μ)=p_s(3+μ)$ for $0<μ<\frac{14}{5}$ and $p_{crit}(3,μ)=p_f(3)$ for $μ\geq\frac{14}{5}$. In the recent paper [16], the authors have obtained the global small solution $u$ for $p>\max\{\frac{5}{3},1+\frac{2}μ\}$ and $μ\geq\frac{14}{5}$. In this paper, by utilizing the hypergeometric Riemann representation and establishing some delicate pointwise spacetime weighted estimates, we prove the global existence of small data radial solution $u$ in the remaining range of $\frac{5}{3}<p\leq1+\frac{2}μ$ and $\frac{14}{5}\leqμ<3$. Therefore, for the radially symmetric case and $μ\geq\frac{14}{5}$, the global existence problem of small data solution $u$ is solved when $p>p_{crit}(3,μ)=\frac{5}{3}$.

AI.tldr: This paper proves global existence of small data radial solutions to the 3D semilinear Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation in the previously open regime 5/3 < p ≤ 1+2/μ with 14/5 ≤ μ < 3, completing the global existence picture for radially symmetric solutions when μ ≥ 14/5.
AI.motivation: For the semilinear Euler-Poisson-Darboux equation in 3D, a critical exponent conjecture identifies when small data solutions blow up vs. exist globally. While blow-up for 1 < p ≤ p_crit has been established, global existence for p > p_crit remained open in certain parameter ranges. This paper aims to close this gap.
AI.method: The authors utilize the hypergeometric Riemann representation for the solution and establish delicate pointwise spacetime weighted estimates to prove global existence of small data radial solutions in the remaining range 5/3 < p ≤ 1+2/μ with 14/5 ≤ μ < 3.
AI.result: The paper proves global existence of small data radial solutions in the previously open parameter range, thereby solving the global existence problem for radially symmetric solutions when μ ≥ 14/5 and p > p_crit(3,μ) = 5/3.
AI.conclusion: For the radially symmetric case with μ ≥ 14/5, the global existence problem for small data solutions is now fully resolved across the entire supercritical range p > 5/3, complementing the previously established blow-up results.

title: Wigner-Eckart Factorization of the Polyatomic Boltzmann Collision Operator
comment: 31 pages, 10 figures, 5 tables. Companion to arXiv:2605.28475. Code: https://github.com/simkinetic/collision-factorization/tree/polyatomic
summary: We extend the Wigner-Eckart factorization of the spectral Boltzmann collision operator to polyatomic gases with continuous internal energy. Because internal energies are invariant under spatial rotations, the SO(3) reduction survives the Borgnakke-Larsen energy exchange, and the twelve-dimensional collision integral collapses onto a nine-dimensional kinematic core. The core splits into a sparse geometric tensor, evaluated exactly, and a dense physical tensor, integrated by singularity-resolving Gauss rules with an auxiliary Laplace representation of the fractional energy couplings. The quadrature attains near machine precision at the fractional exponents of real gases. The collision invariants are embedded exactly, preserving the translational-internal energy exchange. The factorization compresses the operator by three to nearly four orders of magnitude and accelerates its evaluation 40-fold over dense formulations. The method is validated against the exact monatomic limit, Landau-Teller relaxation, and an analytic frozen-channel Prandtl number, and it matches a published calibration of the same kernel for N2, CO, and H2.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the Wigner-Eckart factorization of the spectral Boltzmann collision operator to polyatomic gases with continuous internal energy, reducing a twelve-dimensional collision integral to a nine-dimensional kinematic core, achieving near machine precision and 40-fold acceleration.
AI.motivation: To efficiently handle the spectral Boltzmann collision operator for polyatomic gases with continuous internal energy by exploiting SO(3) symmetry, since internal energies are invariant under spatial rotations.
AI.method: The SO(3) reduction survives the Borgnakke-Larsen energy exchange, collapsing the twelve-dimensional collision integral onto a nine-dimensional kinematic core. The core is split into a sparse geometric tensor (evaluated exactly) and a dense physical tensor (integrated by singularity-resolving Gauss rules with an auxiliary Laplace representation).
AI.result: The factorization compresses the operator by three to nearly four orders of magnitude and accelerates evaluation 40-fold over dense formulations. It attains near machine precision at fractional exponents of real gases, with collision invariants embedded exactly. Validated against monatomic limit, Landau-Teller relaxation, and analytic frozen-channel Prandtl number, matching published calibration for N2, CO, and H2.
AI.conclusion: The method provides an accurate, highly efficient spectral formulation for polyatomic Boltzmann collision operators with continuous internal energy, validated across multiple real gases.

title: Tensor Orthogonal Subspace Split: Theory and Applications
summary: Tensor representations have emerged as a fundamental paradigm for modeling multidimensional data by preserving intrinsic correlations across multiple modes. This paper proposes a novel theoretical framework, termed Tensor Orthogonal Subspace Split (TOSS), which explicitly splits a tensor, along a prescribed mode, into two orthogonal components: a dominant component lying in a prescribed subspace and a residual component lying in the corresponding orthogonal complement. We first present the general formulation of TOSS and systematically investigate its fundamental properties. As an important and practically meaningful special case, we further introduce the rank-one TOSS, which imposes a separable rank-one structure along the splitting mode and admits a clear geometric interpretation. This formulation naturally captures dominant consistent patterns while effectively isolating orthogonal residual component. The proposed framework establishes a unified theoretical foundation for tensor-domain orthogonal split and opens new avenues for structured tensor modeling across diverse applications. Building upon the developed TOSS theory, hyperspectral image restoration and color video background modeling are considered as two representative tasks, for which corresponding optimization models are formulated. Efficient algorithms are developed to solve the resulting problems. Extensive experimental results validate the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Tensor Orthogonal Subspace Split (TOSS), a novel theoretical framework that decomposes a tensor along a prescribed mode into a dominant component lying in a given subspace and a residual component in its orthogonal complement. A rank-one special case with geometric interpretability is also proposed, and the framework is validated through hyperspectral image restoration and color video background modeling tasks.
AI.motivation: Tensor representations are fundamental for modeling multidimensional data, but existing methods lack a unified theoretical framework for orthogonally splitting tensors into structured dominant and residual components, which is needed for applications requiring decomposition into consistent patterns and isolated residuals.
AI.method: The paper (1) formulates the general TOSS framework that splits a tensor along a prescribed mode into two orthogonal components with respect to a specified subspace; (2) introduces rank-one TOSS as a special case that imposes a separable rank-one structure along the splitting mode with clear geometric interpretation; (3) develops optimization models and efficient algorithms for hyperspectral image restoration and color video background modeling based on the TOSS theory.
AI.result: The proposed TOSS framework is validated through extensive experiments on two representative tasks: hyperspectral image restoration and color video background modeling. Results confirm the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed approaches over existing methods.
AI.conclusion: TOSS establishes a unified theoretical foundation for tensor-domain orthogonal splitting, providing a new paradigm for structured tensor modeling with broad applicability across diverse signal and image processing tasks.

title: Global recovery of Lorentzian principal geometry from the hyperbolic Dirichlet-to-Neumann map
summary: We prove that the full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on a finite time interval globally determines the Lorentzian metric \(\mathbf G_{g,c}=-c(x,t)^2\mathrm{d}t^2+g(x)\) encoded by the principal symbol of the wave operator. The result holds in spatial dimensions \(n\geq3\) for multiplicatively separable wave speeds \(c(x,t)=a(x)b(t)\), provided the accumulated effective time during the experiment exceeds the maximal travel time from the boundary to the interior and back. The data determine both the unknown Riemannian metric \(g(x)\) and the wave speed \(c(x,t)\) throughout the observation cylinder, up to a spatial change of coordinates that fixes the boundary and leaves the measured time unchanged. In particular, the temporal factor \(b\) is not prescribed but is recovered from the same measurements. We also construct several examples demonstrating that the dimensional and visibility conditions for uniqueness are sharp.

AI.tldr: The paper proves global uniqueness of the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on a finite time interval for determining both the Riemannian metric and multiplicatively separable wave speed in the wave operator, in spatial dimensions n≥3, subject to an effective time condition exceeding round-trip travel time. The temporal factor is recovered without prior knowledge, and examples show the conditions are sharp.
AI.motivation: To establish that the full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map over a finite time interval globally determines the Lorentzian metric encoded by the wave operator's principal symbol, including recovering the unknown temporal factor of a separable wave speed, and to identify sharp conditions under which such recovery is possible.
AI.method: The proof establishes global uniqueness for the Dirichlet-to-Neumann map in dimensions n≥3 for wave speeds of the form c(x,t)=a(x)b(t), using the accumulated effective time criterion (which must exceed maximal boundary-to-interior-and-back travel time). Boundary-fixing spatial coordinate changes that preserve measured time are used to parametrize uniqueness, with counterexamples constructed to demonstrate sharpness of dimensional and visibility conditions.
AI.result: The full Dirichlet-to-Neumann map on a finite time interval globally determines both the unknown Riemannian metric g(x) and the wave speed c(x,t) throughout the observation cylinder, up to boundary-fixing spatial diffeomorphisms preserving time. The temporal factor b(t) is recovered simultaneously from the same data without being prescribed. Sharpness is established via examples showing the dimensional (n≥3) and visibility (effective time) conditions are necessary.
AI.conclusion: Global uniqueness for the inverse problem holds under separable wave speeds in dimensions n≥3 with sufficient accumulated effective time, recovering both geometric and temporal structure from boundary measurements alone, and the stated conditions are optimal for the result to hold.

title: Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks for viscoelastic fluid equations
summary: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs), inspired by the Kolmogorov Arnold representation theorem, provide an interpretable alternative to multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) by using learnable activation functions on edges rather than fixed node activations. We propose a Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (PI-KAN) framework for solving forward problem of viscoelastic fluid equations, which arise in many complex fluid dynamics applications and are characterized by strong nonlinear coupling between fluid fields. For viscoelastic fluid equations, we adopt the generalized hydrodynamic model, which is well established in the field of dusty plasma. To evaluate the performance of the proposed framework for viscoelastic fluid, we consider benchmark problem based on the Taylor-Green (TG) flow and a modified Taylor-Green flow. We systematically investigate the effects of different network architectures, hyperparameters, and collocation point distributions on the accuracy and convergence behavior of PI-KANs for the range of viscoelastic parameter ($τ_m = 1$--$20$). We also study the impact of random seed initialization on training outcomes. The obtained results provide useful guidance for the design and implementation of physics-informed Kolmogorov-Arnold networks (PI-KANs) in solving viscoelastic fluid equations

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a Physics-Informed Kolmogorov-Arnold Network (PI-KAN) framework for solving forward problems of viscoelastic fluid equations, evaluating its performance on Taylor-Green flow benchmarks and systematically investigating the effects of network architectures, hyperparameters, collocation point distributions, and random seed initialization.
AI.motivation: Viscoelastic fluid equations are characterized by strong nonlinear coupling between fluid fields and are challenging to solve. KANs offer an interpretable alternative to MLPs by using learnable activation functions on edges, and the authors aim to leverage this in a physics-informed framework for viscoelastic fluid problems.
AI.method: The authors propose a PI-KAN framework that integrates KANs with physics-informed constraints to solve viscoelastic fluid equations. They adopt the generalized hydrodynamic model from dusty plasma physics and test on Taylor-Green (TG) flow and a modified TG flow across a viscoelastic parameter range (τ_m = 1-20), systematically studying architectural, hyperparameter, and collocation point effects.
AI.result: The study systematically evaluates the accuracy and convergence behavior of PI-KANs across different network architectures, hyperparameters, collocation point distributions, and viscoelastic parameter values, also assessing the impact of random seed initialization on training outcomes.
AI.conclusion: The results provide practical guidance for designing and implementing PI-KANs for solving viscoelastic fluid equations, offering insights into optimal configurations and training practices.

title: Constraint Preserving AFD-WENO Schemes for Relativistic Hydrodynamics with General Equations of State
summary: We develop a high-order physical-constraint-preserving (PCP) alternative finite difference weighted essentially non-oscillatory (AFD-WENO) scheme for the special relativistic hydrodynamics equations with general equations of state. The proposed scheme comprises two key limiters: a state limiter, which acts after the WENO state interpolation step, and a flux limiter, which acts on the final high-order fluxes. The state limiter ensures that the interpolated states are physically admissible, while the flux limiter ensures that the numerical fluxes are physically admissible. The resulting scheme is rigorously proved to satisfy the physical constraints. Incorporating multiple WENO interpolation techniques, including an improved adaptive-order formulation (WENO-AOI), the method is validated through extensive one- and two-dimensional numerical benchmarks with various equations of state. The numerical results demonstrate high-order accuracy, sharp resolution of discontinuities, and robust stability in extreme relativistic regimes.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a high-order physical-constraint-preserving (PCP) alternative finite difference WENO scheme for special relativistic hydrodynamics with general equations of state, using state and flux limiters to enforce physical admissibility, validated through extensive numerical benchmarks.
AI.motivation: To develop a scheme that simultaneously achieves high-order accuracy, physical constraint preservation, and robust stability for special relativistic hydrodynamics equations with general equations of state, which is challenging due to the nonlinearity of the equations and the need for physical admissibility.
AI.method: The scheme uses two key limiters: a state limiter applied after WENO state interpolation to ensure interpolated states are physically admissible, and a flux limiter applied to the final high-order fluxes to ensure numerical fluxes are physically admissible. It incorporates multiple WENO interpolation techniques, including an improved adaptive-order formulation (WENO-AOI).
AI.result: The scheme is rigorously proven to satisfy physical constraints and validated through extensive 1D and 2D numerical benchmarks with various equations of state, demonstrating high-order accuracy, sharp resolution of discontinuities, and robust stability in extreme relativistic regimes.
AI.conclusion: The proposed PCP AFD-WENO scheme is a reliable and robust high-order method for special relativistic hydrodynamics with general equations of state, delivering physically admissible solutions even in extreme relativistic scenarios.

title: A Liouville type rigidity result for entire solutions of the $k$-Hessian equation
summary: In this note, we prove a Liouville type rigidity result for smooth entire solutions of the $k$-Hessian equation. The proof makes use of a concavity inequality for the $k$-Hessian operator.

AI.tldr: This note proves a Liouville-type rigidity theorem for smooth entire solutions of the k-Hessian equation, using a concavity inequality specific to the k-Hessian operator.
AI.motivation: To establish rigidity (Liouville-type) results for smooth entire solutions of the k-Hessian equation, extending classical results to this general class of fully nonlinear elliptic equations.
AI.method: The proof relies on a concavity inequality for the k-Hessian operator, which is exploited to derive the rigidity conclusion.
AI.result: A Liouville-type rigidity result is established for smooth entire solutions of the k-Hessian equation.
AI.conclusion: The concavity inequality for the k-Hessian operator provides a sufficient tool to prove rigidity of entire smooth solutions.

title: Diffusion-Based Inverse Design of Dielectric Resonator Metasurfaces for Shaping Smart Electromagnetic Environments
summary: Future wireless systems are expected to transform the surrounding space from a passive propagation medium into a smart electromagnetic environment, where engineered surfaces control wave propagation, support wireless sensing, and create programmable electromagnetic fingerprints. A key challenge in realizing this vision is the inverse design of metasurfaces for tailored electromagnetic propagation. While forward analysis evaluates the response of a known geometry, the inverse task starts from a prescribed scattering signature and seeks a physically realizable structure that produces it. This inverse task is inherently nonlinear and often high-dimensional, while candidate solutions may be non-unique and provide no direct indication of practical realizability. Here, we introduce a conditional diffusion framework for inverse design of dielectric resonator metasurfaces from target angular scattering patterns. Trained on T-matrix simulated geometry-response pairs, the model learns a conditional distribution of geometries instead of a deterministic mapping, enabling multiple candidate designs for the ill-posed inverse problem. The best generated metasurface achieves a mean percentage error of 1.39%, outperforming CMA-ES optimization (4.1% after 10 h) while requiring only about one minute for after-training inference. The model also produces lower error distributions than deterministic neural baselines for out-of-distribution spectra, highlighting the potential of diffusion models for efficient metasurface design.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a conditional diffusion framework for inverse design of dielectric resonator metasurfaces, mapping target angular scattering patterns to physically realizable geometries. The model outperforms CMA-ES optimization (1.39% vs 4.1% mean percentage error) while being dramatically faster (~1 minute vs 10 hours), and produces better error distributions than deterministic neural baselines on out-of-distribution data.
AI.motivation: The inverse design of metasurfaces (deriving a geometry from a desired scattering signature) is a critical but challenging problem for future wireless systems with smart electromagnetic environments. This inverse task is inherently nonlinear, high-dimensional, ill-posed with non-unique solutions, and lacks direct indicators of physical realizability.
AI.method: A conditional diffusion model is trained on T-matrix simulated geometry-response pairs. Instead of learning a deterministic mapping, the model learns a conditional distribution of geometries given target angular scattering patterns, enabling generation of multiple candidate designs that address the ill-posed nature of the problem.
AI.result: The best generated metasurface achieves a mean percentage error of 1.39%, outperforming CMA-ES optimization which reached 4.1% after 10 hours. The diffusion model requires only about one minute for after-training inference. It also produces lower error distributions than deterministic neural baselines for out-of-distribution spectra.
AI.conclusion: Diffusion models show strong potential for efficient and effective metasurface inverse design, offering both superior performance and significant computational speedup compared to traditional optimization methods, while also providing robustness for out-of-distribution scenarios.

title: Efficient Hybrid WENO Schemes for Special Relativistic Hydrodynamics with Adaptive Characteristic Reconstruction
summary: Special relativistic hydrodynamics (SRHD) equations arise in the modeling of high-speed fluid flows encountered in astrophysical phenomena such as jets, supernova explosions, and gamma-ray bursts. Owing to their highly nonlinear hyperbolic nature, solutions often develop strong discontinuities, making the design of stable and accurate numerical schemes challenging. Although Weighted Essentially Non-Oscillatory (WENO) schemes are widely used for such problems, component-wise WENO reconstruction may produce spurious oscillations near discontinuities. On the other hand, characteristic-wise WENO reconstruction provides accurate non-oscillatory solutions for systems of conservation laws, but it involves the computation of eigenvectors in each cell, which leads to high computational cost.
